profile.name: Strip the willow
profile.tagline: A high-energy Scottish ceilidh longways dance of continuous linked-arm turns

profile.profile: Strip the willow is a traditional Scottish ceilidh and country dance performed in longways sets. Partners stand in opposing rows, working in continuous arm-linked turns to strip down and up the set until every couple has progressed. Associated historically with the 1734 tune 'Drops of Brandy', it remains one of the most vigorous social dances in modern ceilidh culture.
profile.profile_long:
### Origins and History
Strip the Willow is a Scottish ceilidh dance and country dance performed in longways sets. While popular across Scotland and the wider British Isles, early musical documentation of melodies associated with the dance dates back to the eighteenth century. The tune commonly associated with the dance, known under the title "Drops of Brandy," appears in ten transcriptions on the Tunearch website. The earliest known manuscript transcription of this melody is dated to 1734 within David Young's "Drummond Castle/Duke of Perth Manuscript." The musical lineage of this tune also extends into Irish tradition, notably appearing as entry number 448 in Francis O'Neill's famous 1907 collection, "Dance Music of Ireland: 1001 Gems." Through centuries of social gathering and community celebration, the dance has remained a fixture of Scottish social dancing traditions.

### How It Is Danced
The basic formation for Strip the Willow is a longways set consisting of a row of gentlemen facing a row of ladies as their partners, classically composed of four couples, though sets can extend as long as music permits. The primary structural objective of the dance is to progress the top couple down to the bottom of the set while all other couples move up one position in turn.

The sequence begins with the top couple linking arms and spinning each other at the top of the set for a count of 16 beats. Following this initial spin, the lady performs the first stripping phase down the set. She alternates left-handed anti-clockwise swings with each dancer down the line of men and right-handed clockwise half-turn swings with her own partner as she works steadily down toward the bottom of the line. During this sequence, the top gentleman remains in position, swinging exclusively with his partner between her interactions with the other men.

Upon reaching the bottom of the set, the top couple reunite to join and spin together for a count of 8 beats. The gentleman then executes the second stripping phase, working his way up the line of ladies. He alternates anti-clockwise swings with each lady down the set and clockwise half-turn swings with his partner, while the lady swings only with him.

Once the gentleman returns to the top of the set, the couple join together to spin for a count of 8 beats. They then execute the final joint stripping phase down to the bottom together. During this joint progression, both partners simultaneously turn the other dancers down their respective lines with an anti-clockwise half turn, meeting in the center between each outside turn to execute a clockwise half turn with each other. Upon reaching the bottom one last time, the top couple meet to spin for 8 beats and settle into their new position at the bottom of the set. Simultaneously, the new top couple link arms, spin for 16 beats, and repeat the entire progression.

### Music and Instruments
The rhythmic foundation of Strip the Willow relies on traditional slip jig or compound metre dance tunes, historically linked to the melody "Drops of Brandy." Musical accompaniment at ceilidhs is typically provided by live traditional instruments such as the fiddle, accordion, tin whistle, or full ceilidh bands. The tempo is brisk and continuous to maintain the constant momentum required by the alternating arm turns and longways progression.

### Costume and Setting
Strip the Willow requires no formal specialized dance costume beyond comfortable social wear or traditional Scottish ceilidh attire, such as kilts or tartan garments worn during formal gatherings. The dance takes place in community halls, ballrooms, barn dances, and event spaces with sufficient floor space to accommodate longways lines of dancers.

### Occasions and Meaning
Strip the Willow is performed as a central social figure at ceilidhs, weddings, and community dances. It serves as an inclusive icebreaker and energetic collective celebration, bringing all participants on the floor into physical contact through the continuous chain of arm turns.

### Notable Figures
Historical collectors and transcribers such as David Young, who compiled the 1734 Drummond Castle/Duke of Perth Manuscript, and Francis O'Neill, who published the 1907 collection "Dance Music of Ireland: 1001 Gems," preserved the primary tunes associated with the dance.

### Regional Variants
A prominent regional variant is the Orcadian version, known as the Orcadian Strip the Willow. Best executed in long sets across expansive dance floors, this variation features multiple couples stripping the willow simultaneously. In this version, every fourth or fifth couple strips downwards at the same time while all other couples continuously progress upwards toward the top of the set. Once an ascending couple reaches the top of the line, they wait for the appropriate bar and start another movement. In many modern ceilidhs, the Orcadian Strip the Willow serves as the ultimate dance before Auld Lang Syne is sung.

### Lineage
Strip the Willow belongs to the family of traditional country dances and longways set dances native to the British Isles and Ireland. It maintains deep ties to traditional Scottish ceilidh culture, preserving continuous participatory social partner dancing from the eighteenth century into contemporary global ceilidh practice.

sections.origins_and_history: Strip the Willow is a Scottish ceilidh dance documented through early music transcriptions dating back to the 18th century, notably in David Young's 1734 manuscript and later in Francis O'Neill's 1907 collection.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers form longways sets of partners facing each other. The top couple spins for 16 beats, then the lady strips down the line alternating left-hand turns with opposing men and right-hand turns with her partner. The gentleman repeats the process up the line of ladies, followed by both stripping down the line together.
sections.music_and_instruments: Accompanied by traditional tunes such as 'Drops of Brandy', played on accordion, fiddle, and ceilidh band instruments in energetic compound metre.
sections.costume_and_setting: danced in everyday modern social wear or traditional Scottish attire like kilts in community halls, ballrooms, and ceilidh venues.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed at ceilidhs, weddings, and social gatherings as an inclusive, high-energy group celebration.
sections.notable_figures: David Young (1734 manuscript transcriber) and Francis O'Neill (1907 music collector).
sections.regional_variants: The Orcadian Strip the Willow features multiple couples stripping downwards simultaneously every fourth or fifth position in long sets.
sections.lineage: Part of the Scottish country dance and longways folk set lineage.

basic_steps: Top couple link right arms and spin in the center for 16 beats.
Lady turns line dancer anti-clockwise with left arm, then partner clockwise with right arm.
Gentleman turns line dancer anti-clockwise with left arm, then partner clockwise with right arm.
Both partners simultaneously turn line dancers anti-clockwise and each other clockwise down the set.
teaching.formation: Longways set (line of gentlemen facing line of ladies)
teaching.level_notes: Accessible to beginners; requires stamina for continuous turning.

music_profile.vocal_style: Instrumental dance music, occasionally accompanied by caller prompts or vocal shouts
music_profile.musical_form: AABB repeating structure adjusted to set length
music_profile.sound_description: Energetic, driving accordion and fiddle jigs playing continuous compound-meter melodies like 'Drops of Brandy'.

movement_profile.posture: Upright, active social dance stance with flexible knees and firm elbow connections
movement_profile.footwork: Skip-change step or relaxed rhythmic walking turn step
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Linked elbows (left arm to outside line, right arm to partner)
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Torso rotates smoothly to absorb momentum of continuous turning
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Longways set facing partner across a parallel aisle
movement_profile.partnering: Alternating forearm or linked elbow turns with partner and line members

signature_moves.name: The Willow Strip
signature_moves.description: Alternating left-elbow turn with line dancer and right-elbow turn with partner progressing down the line

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Ground-level traveling turns without high leaps
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Pulling forcefully on partner arms or losing count of arm alternations

learning_units.description: Mastering the alternating arm-link turn progression down a longways set.

social_formats.description: Longways set with couples progressing from top to bottom through arm turns.

beats: Opening on a crowded Scottish ceilidh floor as the fiddle starts 'Drops of Brandy'
Demonstrating the longways set layout and top couple position
Walking through the alternating left-arm and right-arm stripping mechanism
Showcasing the massive multi-couple Orcadian variant
Closing with the full room spinning as the set transitions to Auld Lang Syne

lesson_ladder.goal: Master partner elbow spin for 16 counts
drills: Practice linking right elbows and spinning in place for 16 beats

lesson_ladder.goal: Execute full joint stripping down the set simultaneously
drills: Both partners strip down opposing lines simultaneously without colliding in the aisle

seniors.seated_version: Perform alternating right and left arm links with seated side partners at reduced tempo.
seniors.standing_version: Walk the line turns at half tempo using gentle forearm touches instead of fast elbow spins.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Reduce tempo to 80-90 BPM and limit spin rotation speed.
seniors.counts: Use 8 counts per spin instead of 16 to reduce dizziness.

children.game_version: Run the weaving line game where children high-five alternating side partners down the track.
